beats.caption: EEPROM: a tiny chip that remembers settings
beats.text: Small serial EEPROMs, often a few kilobits, sit on boards, DIMMs, sensors and cars. They hold configuration, serial numbers and calibration that must survive power-off and change now and then.

beats.caption: Each bit is a select transistor plus a floating gate
beats.text: Cut open, an EEPROM bit is two transistors. The floating-gate cell stores charge like flash; the select transistor beside it isolates that cell, so one byte can be changed without touching its neighbours.

beats.caption: Write: electrons tunnel onto one byte's gates
beats.text: The select transistor opens a single byte, and a high voltage pulls electrons through a thin tunnel oxide onto the floating gate. Only that byte changes; there is no block erase as in flash.

beats.caption: Erase electrically, byte by byte, no UV lamp
beats.text: Reversing the field tunnels the charge back off. Older EPROMs needed a UV lamp through a quartz window to erase; EEPROM does it with voltage in milliseconds, for about a million cycles.

beats.caption: Flexible but big: the extra transistor costs density
beats.text: Two transistors per bit makes EEPROM far less dense than flash, so it stays at kilobits to a few megabits for config data. Makers: Microchip (MCHP), STMicroelectronics (STM), Infineon (IFX.DE).
